2 Corinthians — Book introduction (Modern English candidate)

Paul's second letter to the Corinthians was written probably about a year after the first.

Its contents are closely connected with that earlier letter.

Paul considered how his earlier message had been received. The response gave him reason to thank God, who enabled him to fulfill his responsibility toward the believers.

Many Corinthians showed signs of repentance and improved their conduct.

Others, however, continued following false teachers.

Paul delayed visiting the church because he did not want to discipline them severely before giving them an opportunity to change.

Some then accused him of unreliability and inconsistency.

They also attacked him as proud, self-glorifying and harsh, speaking about him contemptuously.

Nevertheless, this letter shows the same deep affection for the Corinthian believers that appeared in the first, the same concern for the gospel's honor and the same courage in correcting their sins.

The first six chapters are mainly practical.

The remaining chapters address the Corinthian church's particular circumstances more directly, while still providing instruction useful to Christians everywhere.

Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesThe apostle blesses God for comfort in, and deliverance out of troubles.1–11He professes his own and his fellow-labourers' integrity.12–14Gives reasons for his not coming to them.15–24
God comforts us and enables us to comfort others (verses 1–11)

We are encouraged to come confidently to the throne of grace to receive mercy and find the help we need.

The Lord can give peace to a troubled conscience and calm the most violent passions of the soul. He gives these blessings as the Father of his redeemed family.

Our Savior himself tells us not to let our hearts be troubled.

Every true comfort comes from God, and our sweetest comforts are found in him.

He speaks peace to the soul through the free forgiveness of sins. He also comforts us through the life-giving work of the Holy Spirit and the abundant mercy of his grace.

He heals broken hearts, binds up painful wounds and gives hope and joy even amid the heaviest sorrows.

God does not comfort us merely to make us happier. He also intends his gifts to make us useful to other people. He provides enough comfort to sustain those who sincerely trust and serve him.

Even when suffering brings us to the point of despairing of life itself, we may trust the God who is able to bring people back from death.

That trust does not disappoint.

Remembering deliverance in the past strengthens our faith and hope for the future. Earlier mercies place us under an obligation to trust the Lord again.

We also owe one another more than prayers for relief. We should join in praise and thanksgiving when prayers are answered, giving thanks to God for benefits received.

In this way both our trials and the mercies that follow them may become blessings to ourselves and to others.

Paul appeals to the integrity of his conduct (verses 12–14)

Paul knew that, considered as a sinner, he had no ground for boasting except Jesus Christ.

But as a believer, he could rightly rejoice that his conduct agreed with the faith he professed.

Conscience bears witness not merely to an isolated action but to the settled direction and pattern of a person's life.

We should therefore examine our conduct as a whole, rather than judging ourselves by one good or bad act taken alone.

A life is properly ordered when it proceeds from a principle of grace within the heart.

With such a conscience, we can entrust our reputation to the Lord.

Nevertheless, there are times when we should take suitable steps to clear our name, especially when the honor of the gospel or our ability to serve others depends upon it.

Why Paul changed his travel plans (verses 15–24)

Paul answered the accusation that his failure to visit Corinth showed him to be fickle or unreliable.

Faithful Christians should guard their reputation for sincerity and steadiness.

They should make decisions carefully and not change them without substantial reasons.

God's own promises never become less certain because human plans change.

They are given through Jesus Christ and are confirmed by the extraordinary works God accomplished in his Son's life, resurrection and ascension.

The Holy Spirit establishes believers firmly in gospel faith.

His life-giving work is a pledge of everlasting life, while his consolations anticipate everlasting joy.

Paul delayed his visit because he hoped to spare the Corinthians the painful rebuke he might otherwise have needed to administer before seeing the effect of his first letter.

Our spiritual strength comes through faith, and so must our joy and comfort.

Faith is accompanied by holy dispositions and the fruits of grace.

These fruits help protect us against self-deception in a matter so important.
classic_reading:
[2Cor.1.1-2Cor.1.11]
2 Corinthians
The second epistle to the Corinthians probably was written about a year after the first. Its contents are closely connected with those of the former epistle. The manner in which the letter St. Paul formerly wrote had been received, is particularly noticed; this was such as to fill his heart with gratitude to God, who enabled him fully to discharge his duty towards them. Many had shown marks of repentance, and amended their conduct, but others still followed their false teachers; and as the apostle delayed his visit, from his unwillingness to treat them with severity, they charged him with levity and change of conduct. Also, with pride, vain-glory, and severity, and they spake of him with contempt. In this epistle we find the same ardent affection towards the disciples at Corinth, as in the former, the same zeal for the honour of the gospel, and the same boldness in giving Christian reproof. The first six chapters are chiefly practical: the rest have more reference to the state of the Corinthian church, but they contain many rules of general application.
Chapter 1
Chapter Outline
The apostle blesses God for comfort in, and deliverance out of troubles. | (1-11) |
He professes his own and his fellow-labourers' integrity.
(12-14)
Gives reasons for his not coming to them. | (15-24) |
Verses 1-11
We are encouraged to come boldly to the throne of grace, that we may obtain mercy, and find grace to help in time of need. The Lord is able to give peace to the troubled conscience, and to calm the raging passions of the soul. These blessings are given by him, as the Father of his redeemed family. It is our Saviour who says, Let not your heart be troubled. All comforts come from God, and our sweetest comforts are in him. He speaks peace to souls by granting the free remission of sins; and he comforts them by the enlivening influences of the Holy Spirit, and by the rich mercies of his grace. He is able to bind up the broken-hearted, to heal the most painful wounds, and also to give hope and joy under the heaviest sorrows. The favours God bestows on us, are not only to make us cheerful, but also that we may be useful to others. He sends comforts enough to support such as simply trust in and serve him. If we should be brought so low as to despair even of life, yet we may then trust God, who can bring back even from death. Their hope and trust were not in vain; nor shall any be ashamed who trust in the Lord. Past experiences encourage faith and hope, and lay us under obligation to trust in God for time to come. And it is our duty, not only to help one another with prayer, but in praise and thanksgiving, and thereby to make suitable returns for benefits received. Thus both trials and mercies will end in good to ourselves and others.
[2Cor.1.12-2Cor.1.14]
Verses 12-14
Though, as a sinner, the apostle could only rejoice and glory in Christ Jesus, yet, as a believer, he might rejoice and glory in being really what he professed. Conscience witnesses concerning the steady course and tenor of the life. Thereby we may judge ourselves, and not by this or by that single act. Our conversation will be well ordered, when we live and act under such a gracious principle in the heart. Having this, we may leave our characters in the Lord's hands, but using proper means to clear them, when the credit of the gospel, or our usefulness, calls for it.
[2Cor.1.15-2Cor.1.24]
Verses 15-24
The apostle clears himself from the charge of levity and inconstancy, in not coming to Corinth. Good men should be careful to keep the reputation of sincerity and constancy; they should not resolve, but on careful thought; and they will not change unless for weighty reasons. Nothing can render God's promises more certain: his giving them through Christ, assures us they are his promises; as the wonders God wrought in the life, resurrection, and ascension of his Son, confirm faith. The Holy Spirit makes Christians firm in the faith of the gospel: the quickening of the Spirit is an earnest of everlasting life; and the comforts of the Spirit are an earnest of everlasting joy. The apostle desired to spare the blame he feared would be unavoidable, if he had gone to Corinth before he learned what effect his former letter produced. Our strength and ability are owing to faith; and our comfort and joy must flow from faith. The holy tempers and gracious fruits which attend faith, secure from delusion in so important a matter.

Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesReasons for the apostle not coming to Corinth.1–4Directions about restoring the repentant offender.5–11An account of his labours and success in spreading the gospel of Christ.12–17
Paul explains his reluctance to bring sorrow (verses 1–4)

Paul wanted his next visit to Corinth to be a joyful meeting rather than an occasion for painful confrontation.

He wrote his earlier letter trusting that the Corinthians would respond in ways that were good for them and comforting to him.

He hoped they would gladly remove the causes of distress between them.

We should never take pleasure in causing another person pain, even when our responsibilities require us to give a warning or correction that hurts.

Necessary discipline should be undertaken reluctantly, from love and for the other person's good.

Forgive and restore the repentant offender (verses 5–11)

Paul called the Corinthians to restore to fellowship the person who had done wrong.

That person had recognized the offense and had been deeply distressed by the correction already received.

Even grief over sin must not be allowed to make people unable to perform their remaining duties or drive them into hopeless despair.

Satan can take advantage of excessive severity by persuading a penitent person to think harshly of God and of religion, until that person loses hope altogether.

The enemy can also use the church's refusal to forgive as a weapon against Christ's congregations and ministers.

When Christians appear unforgiving, their public witness suffers, divisions arise and the gospel's ministry is hindered.

Therefore correction requires wisdom.

Church leaders must avoid two opposite errors: tolerating wrongdoing as though it were harmless, and treating repentant sinners with excessive harshness.

Satan has many schemes and knows how to use even our mistakes to cause harm.

The gospel triumphs through Christ (verses 12–17)

Every victory enjoyed by a Christian comes through Jesus Christ, who deserves all the honor and praise.

When the gospel spreads and bears fruit, believers have good reason to rejoice.

In ancient victory processions, sweet-smelling perfumes were spread around the participants.

Similarly, the name and salvation of Jesus are like fragrant ointment poured out wherever his gospel is proclaimed.

But people respond differently to this fragrance.

For some, the gospel becomes an aroma of death leading to death. They reject it and are ruined by that refusal.

For others it becomes an aroma of life leading to life. It awakens people who were spiritually dead in sins, continues strengthening their spiritual life and finally brings them to everlasting life.

Paul felt the dreadful seriousness of this task.

We should share that concern.

The ministry is far greater than our personal abilities. We have no sufficient strength in ourselves; our sufficiency comes from God.

Everything we do in religion must be done sincerely and consciously before God.

What is done for show or through dishonest motives does not come from him and cannot be acceptable to him.

May we watch our motives and seek the inward witness of conscience, instructed by the Holy Spirit, so that we speak in Christ and of Christ with genuine sincerity.

[2Cor.2.1-2Cor.2.4]
Chapter 2
Chapter Outline
Reasons for the apostle not coming to Corinth. | (1-4) |
Directions about restoring the repentant offender. | (5-11) |
An account of his labours and success in spreading the gospel of Christ. | (12-17) |
Verses 1-4
The apostle desired to have a cheerful meeting with them; and he had written in confidence of their doing what was to their benefit and his comfort; and that therefore they would be glad to remove every cause of disquiet from him. We should always give pain unwillingly, even when duty requires that it must be given.
[2Cor.2.5-2Cor.2.11]
Verses 5-11
The apostle desires them to receive the person who had done wrong, again into their communion; for he was aware of his fault, and much afflicted under his punishment. Even sorrow for sin should not unfit for other duties, and drive to despair. Not only was there danger last Satan should get advantage, by tempting the penitent to hard thoughts of God and religion, and so drive him to despair; but against the churches and the ministers of Christ, by bringing an evil report upon Christians as unforgiving; thus making divisions, and hindering the success of the ministry. In this, as in other things, wisdom is to be used, that the ministry may not be blamed for indulging sin on the one hand, or for too great severity towards sinners on the other hand. Satan has many plans to deceive, and knows how to make a bad use of our mistakes.
[2Cor.2.12-2Cor.2.17]
Verses 12-17
A believer's triumphs are all in Christ. To him be the praise and glory of all, while the success of the gospel is a good reason for a Christian's joy and rejoicing. In ancient triumphs, abundance of perfumes and sweet odours were used; so the name and salvation of Jesus, as ointment poured out, was a sweet savour diffused in every place. Unto some, the gospel is a savour of death unto death. They reject it to their ruin. Unto others, the gospel is a savour of life unto life: as it quickened them at first when they were dead in trespasses and sins, so it makes them more lively, and will end in eternal life. Observe the awful impressions this matter made upon the apostle, and should also make upon us. The work is great, and of ourselves we have no strength at all; all our sufficiency is of God. But what we do in religion, unless it is done in sincerity, as in the sight of God, is not of God, does not come from him, and will not reach to him. May we carefully watch ourselves in this matter; and seek the testimony of our consciences, under the teaching of the Holy Spirit, that as of sincerity, so speak we in Christ and of Christ.

Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesThe preference of the gospel to the law given by Moses.1–11The preaching of the apostle was suitable to the excellency and evidence of the gospel, through the power of the Holy Ghost.12–18
The gospel brings greater glory than the ministry of the law (verses 1–11)

Humble, spiritually minded people dislike even the appearance of praising themselves or seeking human applause.

Faithful ministers find their greatest joy and the best testimony to their work in the changed hearts and lives of the people they serve.

The Corinthians themselves were evidence of Christ's work through Paul's ministry.

Christ's law was written upon their hearts, and his love had been poured into them.

This message was not engraved on stone tablets, as the law given through Moses had been.

It was written on living, softened human hearts (Ezekiel 36:26).

Henry draws an important distinction: the hearts are fleshy, meaning soft and receptive, not fleshly, meaning governed by sinful appetites.

The Holy Spirit's creative and renewing power softened those hearts so that they could receive Christ's law.

All the glory belongs to God.

Our entire dependence is upon him, so all the praise must be his as well.

The letter kills, but the Spirit gives life.

The written law exposes sin and announces its curse and death.

But merely possessing the outward words or forms of the gospel also leaves a person unchanged when the Holy Spirit does not give life through them.

The old covenant ministry revealed human guilt and God's just anger.

The gospel reveals grace and Emmanuel, God with us.

It shows the righteousness God provides through faith and explains the mercy and forgiveness available through Jesus Christ, leading to eternal life.

The glory of this gospel far exceeds that of the Mosaic dispensation, as a brighter light outshines a lesser one.

But even the New Testament becomes merely a dead letter when treated only as a religious system or external form, without dependence on the Spirit's power to awaken and transform the soul.

The veil is removed and believers are transformed (verses 12–18)

Ministers of the gospel should speak plainly and clearly.

Believers living under the old covenant saw only partial and passing glimpses of the Savior's glory.

Unbelievers often stopped at the visible ceremonies and did not look beyond them.

But the gospel openly calls us to believe, love and obey.

The message of Christ crucified has been stated as clearly as human language can express it.

Under the law, a veil lay upon people's hearts.

That veil is removed by the biblical teaching concerning Christ when God converts a person to himself.

The ignorance that once obscured the heart is lifted.

Those who believe and enjoy the gospel receive wonderful freedom: they can now delight in walking according to God's commandments.

They see the glory of the Lord without the former veil.

Christians should cherish these privileges and make full use of them.

But we must not be satisfied with knowing doctrines without experiencing the transforming work of the Spirit.

His work makes us increasingly like the character and purpose of Christ's glorious gospel and unites us more closely to our Lord and Savior.

Through Scripture we behold Christ as in a mirror.

Just as reflected light causes a face to shine, looking upon the Lord by faith changes believers so that his glory begins to shine in their lives.
classic_reading:
[2Cor.3.1-2Cor.3.11]
Chapter 3
Chapter Outline
The preference of the gospel to the law given by Moses. | (1-11) |
The preaching of the apostle was suitable to the excellency and evidence of the gospel, through the power of the Holy Ghost. | (12-18) |
Verses 1-11
Even the appearance of self-praise and courting human applause, is painful to the humble and spiritual mind. Nothing is more delightful to faithful ministers, or more to their praise, than the success of their ministry, as shown in the spirits and lives of those among whom they labour. The law of Christ was written in their hearts, and the love of Christ shed abroad there. Nor was it written in tables of stone, as the law of God given to Moses, but on the fleshy (not fleshly, as fleshliness denotes sensuality) tables of the heart, [Ezek.36.26] Eze 36:26. Their hearts were humbled and softened to receive this impression, by the new-creating power of the Holy Spirit. He ascribes all the glory to God. And remember, as our whole dependence is upon the Lord, so the whole glory belongs to him alone. The letter killeth: the letter of the law is the ministration of death; and if we rest only in the letter of the gospel, we shall not be the better for so doing: but the Holy Spirit gives life spiritual, and life eternal. The Old Testament dispensation was the ministration of death, but the New Testament of life. The law made known sin, and the wrath and curse of God; it showed us a God above us, and a God against us; but the gospel makes known grace, and Emmanuel, God with us. Therein the righteousness of God by faith is revealed; and this shows us that the just shall live by his faith; this makes known the grace and mercy of God through Jesus Christ, for obtaining the forgiveness of sins and eternal life. The gospel so much exceeds the law in glory, that it eclipses the glory of the legal dispensation. But even the New Testament will be a killing letter, if shown as a mere system or form, and without dependence on God the Holy Spirit, to give it a quickening power.
[2Cor.3.12-2Cor.3.18]
Verses 12-18
It is the duty of the ministers of the gospel to use great plainness, or clearness, of speech. The Old Testament believers had only cloudy and passing glimpses of that glorious Saviour, and unbelievers looked no further than to the outward institution. But the great precepts of the gospel, believe, love, obey, are truths stated as clearly as possible. And the whole doctrine of Christ crucified, is made as plain as human language can make it. Those who lived under the law, had a veil upon their hearts. This veil is taken away by the doctrines of the Bible about Christ. When any person is converted to God, then the veil of ignorance is taken away. The condition of those who enjoy and believe the gospel is happy, for the heart is set at liberty to run the ways of God's commandments. They have light, and with open face they behold the glory of the Lord. Christians should prize and improve these privileges. We should not rest contented without knowing the transforming power of the gospel, by the working of the Spirit, bringing us to seek to be like the temper and tendency of the glorious gospel of our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ, and into union with Him. We behold Christ, as in the glass of his word; and as the reflection from a mirror causes the face to shine, the faces of Christians shine also.

Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesThe apostles laboured with much diligence, sincerity, and faithfulness.1–7Their sufferings for the gospel were great, yet with rich supports.8–12Prospects of eternal glory keep believers from fainting under troubles.13–18
Faithful ministry and treasure in fragile vessels (verses 1–7)

Even the best people would lose heart if they did not receive God's mercy.

But the mercy that has helped us through earlier difficulties and sustained us until now can be trusted to sustain us to the end.

The apostles did not hide dishonorable purposes beneath a convincing appearance of goodness. They did not make the gospel ministry a tool for personal advantage.

People who live sincerely and uprightly will generally retain the respect of wise and good observers.

Through the gospel, Christ reveals his glory to human minds.

But the devil's purpose is to keep people in ignorance. Since he cannot prevent the gospel's light from entering the world, he strives to keep individuals away from it or set their hearts against it.

Henry traces rejection of the gospel to the deliberate blindness and wickedness of the human heart.

The apostles did not preach to exalt themselves or make themselves the center of the message.

They proclaimed Jesus Christ as Savior and Deliverer, the One who saves completely everyone who comes to God through him.

Ministers are servants for people's spiritual good, but that does not mean becoming servants of their passing moods or sinful desires.

Seeing sunlight fill the sky is wonderful. But the light of the gospel shining into a human heart is even more wonderful and beneficial.

Light marked the beginning of the original creation. Likewise, the Holy Spirit's first work in a person's new creation is to shine spiritual light into the soul.

Yet this treasure of gospel truth and grace has been placed in earthen vessels.

Christian ministers share the weaknesses, temptations and emotions of other people.

God could have commissioned angels to announce the gospel, or chosen the most highly admired people in the world.

Instead, he chose comparatively weak and unimpressive instruments.

This made the Lord's power more evident, both in sustaining his ministers and in transforming the people who received their message.

Severe suffering sustained by grace (verses 8–12)

The apostles experienced extraordinary suffering, yet they also received extraordinary support.

Friends may abandon believers, and enemies may persecute them.

But God will not leave or forsake his people.

There may be inner fears as well as outward conflicts. Nevertheless, God's servants are not destroyed.

Paul described their sufferings as reflecting the sufferings of Jesus Christ.

Through them, the power of Christ's resurrection and the grace flowing from the living Savior could also become visible.

Compared with the apostles' hardships, many other Christians at that time enjoyed relatively comfortable circumstances.

The contrast should make those of us living in ease thankful rather than indifferent to the sufferings of faithful servants.

Eternal glory outweighs present trouble (verses 13–18)

Faith is an effective remedy against faintheartedness in affliction.

The apostles knew that Christ had been raised and that his resurrection guaranteed their own.

This hope gives courage in suffering and lifts believers above the fear of death.

Their trials also served the church's good and God's glory.

A minister can serve the church not only through preaching and conduct but even through suffering endured faithfully.

The hope of everlasting life was the apostles' comfort and support.

What physical sight might judge to be heavy, long and unbearable, faith recognized as light and momentary when measured against what lay ahead.

All temporal affliction becomes light in comparison with the immeasurable weight of eternal glory.

If Paul could describe his many severe and prolonged trials as light and brief in this sense, how should we view our comparatively small difficulties?

Faith teaches us to judge both present suffering and eternal hope correctly.

Some things are visible; others are unseen.

The unseen realities of God's promised future are eternal, whereas the visible things of this world are temporary.

Let us stop making earthly advantages our highest ambition or present suffering our greatest fear.

Instead, let us diligently seek assurance of the everlasting happiness God promises his people.
classic_reading:
[2Cor.4.1-2Cor.4.7]
Chapter 4
Chapter Outline
The apostles laboured with much diligence, sincerity, and faithfulness.
(1-7)
Their sufferings for the gospel were great, yet with rich supports.
(8-12)
Prospects of eternal glory keep believers from fainting under troubles.
(13-18)
Verses 1-7
The best of men would faint, if they did not receive mercy from God. And that mercy which has helped us out, and helped us on, hitherto, we may rely upon to help us even to the end. The apostles had no base and wicked designs, covered with fair and specious pretences. They did not try to make their ministry serve a turn. Sincerity or uprightness will keep the favourable opinion of wise and good men. Christ by his gospel makes a glorious discovery to the minds of men. But the design of the devil is, to keep men in ignorance; and when he cannot keep the light of the gospel of Christ out of the world, he spares no pains to keep men from the gospel, or to set them against it. The rejection of the gospel is here traced to the wilful blindness and wickedness of the human heart. Self was not the matter or the end of the apostles' preaching; they preached Christ as Jesus, the Saviour and Deliverer, who saves to the uttermost all that come to God through him. Ministers are servants to the souls of men; they must avoid becoming servants to the humours or the lusts of men. It is pleasant to behold the sun in the firmament; but it is more pleasant and profitable for the gospel to shine in the heart. As light was the beginning of the first creation; so, in the new creation, the light of the Spirit is his first work upon the soul. The treasure of gospel light and grace is put into earthen vessels. The ministers of the gospel are subject to the same passions and weaknesses as other men. God could have sent angels to make known the glorious doctrine of the gospel, or could have sent the most admired sons of men to teach the nations, but he chose humbler, weaker vessels, that his power might be more glorified in upholding them, and in the blessed change wrought by their ministry.
[2Cor.4.8-2Cor.4.12]
Verses 8-12
The apostles were great sufferers, yet they met with wonderful support. Believers may be forsaken of their friends, as well as persecuted by enemies; but their God will never leave them nor forsake them. There may be fears within, as well as fightings without; yet we are not destroyed. The apostle speaks of their sufferings as a counterpart of the sufferings of Christ, that people might see the power of Christ's resurrection, and of grace in and from the living Jesus. In comparison with them, other Christians were, even at that time, in prosperous circumstances.
[2Cor.4.13-2Cor.4.18]
Verses 13-18
The grace of faith is an effectual remedy against fainting in times of trouble. They knew that Christ was raised, and that his resurrection was an earnest and assurance of theirs. The hope of this resurrection will encourage in a suffering day, and set us above the fear of death. Also, their sufferings were for the advantage of the church, and to God's glory. The sufferings of Christ's ministers, as well as their preaching and conversation, are for the good of the church and the glory of God. The prospect of eternal life and happiness was their support and comfort. What sense was ready to pronounce heavy and long, grievous and tedious, faith perceived to be light and short, and but for a moment. The weight of all temporal afflictions was lightness itself, while the glory to come was a substance, weighty, and lasting beyond description. If the apostle could call his heavy and long-continued trials light, and but for a moment, what must our trifling difficulties be! Faith enables to make this right judgment of things. There are unseen things, as well as things that are seen. And there is this vast difference between them; unseen things are eternal, seen things but temporal, or temporary only. Let us then look off from the things which are seen; let us cease to seek for worldly advantages, or to fear present distresses. Let us give diligence to make our future happiness sure.

modern_osis:
Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesThe apostle's hope and desire of heavenly glory.1–8This excited to diligence. The reasons of his being affected with zeal for the Corinthians.9–15The necessity of regeneration, and of reconciliation with God through Christ.16–21
Our future home and the presence of Christ (verses 1–8)

Faith assures the believer that life does not end at the grave.

Through God's grace, we also possess a solid hope of heaven as our home, place of rest and shelter.

Our Father's house has many dwelling places. God himself is its Architect and Builder.

Heaven's joy is what God has prepared for those who love him.

Our present bodies are like temporary tents or poor houses of clay, decaying and slowly collapsing on foundations of dust.

The body can feel like a heavy burden, especially when sickness and suffering come.

But believers groan most deeply because of the body of sin—the corrupt desires that still remain within them and continually trouble their souls.

Death will remove our earthly bodies and comforts, and it will end the outward troubles of this life.

But believers will be clothed with praise, righteousness and glory.

The Holy Spirit's present graces and comforts are pledges of the everlasting life and consolation ahead.

God is already with us through his Spirit and his appointed means of grace. Yet this is not the same as being with him in the full way we hope to enjoy in heaven.

Now we live by faith; there we shall live by sight.

Until then, it is both our duty and our good to continue walking by faith.

These verses clearly teach the happiness enjoyed by the souls of believers when they are absent from their bodies and present where Jesus reveals his glory.

We are bound both to our present bodies and to our Lord.

Each has a claim upon our affections.

But how much more powerfully does Christ call the souls he has loved, chosen and received from the Father to be united closely with himself!

Compared with being separated from the Lord, why should death itself be our greatest fear?

Future judgment and Christ's love inspire service (verses 9–15)

The hope of heaven should stir us toward greater effort and obedience, never toward laziness or sinful complacency.

Remember the coming judgment—the solemn terror of the Lord.

Knowing how dreadful the Lord's vengeance will be against those who persist in evil, Paul and his companions used every proper argument and appeal to persuade people to believe in Jesus and live as his disciples.

Their zeal served God's honor and the welfare of the church.

Christ's love will produce similar devotion in us when we consider it carefully.

All humanity was lost, dead in sins, enslaved to evil and unable to rescue itself.

Without Christ's death, we would have remained in that miserable condition forever.

Therefore the goal of our living and acting must not be ourselves but Christ.

A Christian's life belongs to him.

Sadly, many show that their professed faith and love are hollow by continuing to live entirely for themselves and this world.

A new creation reconciled to God through Christ (verses 16–21)

A renewed person lives by new principles, follows new rules, seeks new ends and keeps new company.

The believer becomes a new creation.

The heart is not merely repaired or adjusted; God gives an entirely new heart.

We are God's workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works.

We remain the same human beings, yet our character and conduct are transformed.

Regeneration means much more than an external improvement in behavior.

Someone who once saw no beauty in Christ and felt no desire for him now loves the Savior above everything.

Before regeneration, the heart is hostile to God, and God is justly offended by sin.

Yet reconciliation is possible.

Through Jesus Christ, the God whom we have offended has reconciled us to himself.

By divine inspiration the Scriptures were written as the message of reconciliation, announcing that peace has been made through the cross and explaining how we can receive its blessings.

God gains nothing from our hostility or our reconciliation; he loses nothing if we remain enemies.

Nevertheless, he graciously appeals to sinners to lay aside their hostility and accept his salvation.

Christ knew no sin.

Yet he was made sin for us—not made a sinner, but made a sin offering, a sacrifice for sin.

And though God is with us here, by his Spirit, and in his ordinances, yet we are not with him as we hope to be. Faith is for this world, and sight is for the other world. It is our duty, and it will be our interest, to walk by faith, till we live by sight. This shows clearly the happiness to be enjoyed by the souls of believers when absent from the body, and where Jesus makes known his glorious presence. We are related to the body and to the Lord; each claims a part in us. But how much more powerfully the Lord pleads for having the soul of the believer closely united with himself! Their zeal and diligence were for the glory of God and the good of the church. Christ's love to us will have a like effect upon us, if duly considered and rightly judged. All were lost and undone, dead and ruined, slaves to sin, having no power to deliver themselves, and must have remained thus miserable for ever, if Christ had not died. The gospel is a word of grace sounding in our ears.

The present time is the day of salvation: the gospel is offered, the means of grace are provided, and God's saving invitation can be received now.

We have a day of grace today. Let us not neglect it.

Ministers should remember that they are God's servants and behave in every circumstance as people entrusted with his work.

Believers also need God's grace when people speak well of them or speak against them.

They need grace to receive approval without becoming proud, and to bear criticism with patience.

Money once wasted recklessly is saved. Time once spent in harmful pursuits is put to constructive work.

Here unbelievers means those who do not have genuine saving faith.

The harmful consequences of ignoring Scripture's warnings concerning marriage can be very serious.

A marriage that was meant to provide a suitable helper can instead become a trap.

Henry makes an important qualification: people already bound in such a marriage without having deliberately chosen to disregard God's command may look to him for consolation under that cross.

But believers who willingly enter those unions despite Scripture's warnings should expect considerable distress.

The warning also extends to ordinary social relationships.

Henry counsels believers not to choose wicked people as their closest companions, while explicitly recognizing that it is impossible to avoid every encounter, conversation or shared situation with them.

If it is considered a wonderful privilege to be the son or daughter of an earthly ruler, how much greater is the dignity and happiness of being a son or daughter of Almighty God!

Instead of a help meet, the union brings a snare. Those whose cross it is to be unequally united, without their wilful fault, may expect consolation under it; but when believers enter into such unions, against the express warnings of God's word, they must expect must distress. The caution also extends to common conversation. We should not join in friendship and acquaintance with wicked men and unbelievers. Though we cannot wholly avoid seeing and hearing, and being with such, yet we should never choose them for friends. We must not defile ourselves by converse with those who defile themselves with sin. Pursuing holiness and receiving faithful ministers (verses 1–4)

God's promises give us strong reasons to pursue holiness.

We must cleanse ourselves from everything that defiles the body and the spirit.

If we hope in God as our Father, we should desire to become holy as he is holy and to resemble our heavenly Father.

Only his grace, working by the Holy Spirit, can truly cleanse us.

Nevertheless, growth in holiness should be the constant object of our prayers and efforts.

It is dangerous when people regard gospel ministers as contemptible, because contempt for the messenger may lead to contempt for the gospel.

Ministers must not flatter anyone, but they should show gentleness toward everyone.

They may ask for esteem and goodwill when they can honestly say that they have corrupted no one through false teaching or flattering words, defrauded no one, and never pursued their own advantage at another person's expense.

Paul's great affection for the Corinthians moved him to speak freely to them.

That affection also led him to speak proudly of their progress wherever he went.

Godly sorrow leads to genuine repentance (verses 5–11)

Paul and his companions faced conflict outside and fears within.

They met opposition from both Jews and Gentiles, while also carrying deep anxiety for people who had embraced the Christian faith.

But God comforts those who are downcast.

We should look beyond the human means through which comfort arrives and recognize God as the source of every true consolation and blessing.

There is a profound difference between godly sorrow and the sorrow of this world.

Sorrow that agrees with God's will, seeks his glory and is produced by the Holy Spirit makes the heart humble, contrite and submissive.

It moves the believer to put sin to death and walk in newness of life.

This repentance belongs with saving faith in Jesus Christ and participation in the blessings of his atoning sacrifice.

Worldly regret can mourn consequences without turning from sin.

But genuine repentance bears visible fruit.

When the heart changes, the life and actions change.

The Corinthians' repentance produced indignation against sin, against their own past conduct, and against the tempter and his agents.

It produced watchfulness and a careful fear of falling into sin again.

It brought a strong desire to be reconciled to God.

It stirred zeal for duty and opposition to wrongdoing.

It also prompted practical attempts to correct the harm their sins had caused.

Deep humility before God, hatred of all sin, faith in Christ, a new heart and a new life together characterize the repentance that leads to salvation.

May the Lord grant this repentance to each of us.

Mutual encouragement through Titus and the Corinthians (verses 12–16)

Paul's confidence in the Corinthians had not been disappointed.

He had shared that confidence with Titus, and the good news now allowed him to look toward their future with joy.

This passage teaches the mutual responsibilities of pastors and congregations.

Believers should ease the difficulties of pastoral service by showing respect and willing obedience.

Pastors, in turn, should care faithfully for their people and encourage them by expressing satisfaction, joy, affection and tenderness when they respond well.

We must recognize the grace of God as the source of every genuinely good quality in us and every good deed we accomplish.

It is a great gift from God to be made useful to others and eager to participate in good work.

Paul praised the generosity of the Macedonian believers.

They did not have to be pressured to contribute. They actually pleaded with Paul to accept their gift.

Whatever we spend in God's service, we are merely returning to him something that already belongs to him.

But our contributions will not be accepted by God or truly benefit us unless we first give ourselves to the Lord.

Acknowledging divine grace as the source of good works both honors their true Giver and teaches us where to find the strength to perform them.

Spiritual joy expands the heart and moves it to loving service.

How different this is from people who refuse to join any good undertaking unless others press them repeatedly!

Christ's generosity is our greatest example (verses 7–9)

Faith is the root of a life that pleases God (Hebrews 11:6).

Those who abound in faith should also grow in other graces and good works, especially those motivated by love.

People who talk the most are not always the most active in doing good.

But the Corinthians had already shown diligence in understanding and speaking about the faith, as well as in putting it into practice.

Paul urged them to add another grace to these virtues: generous care for poor believers.

The greatest reasons for fulfilling our Christian duties come from the grace and love of Jesus Christ.

Christ was rich because he was God, equal with the Father in power and glory.

Yet he not only became human for our sake; he also became poor.

He humbled himself to the point of offering his life upon the cross as a sacrifice to ransom our souls.

From what glory to what poverty our blessed Lord descended for us!

And through his poverty, what riches he has opened to us!

Our greatest happiness is to belong entirely to him and be available for his service.

Finish the generous work you began (verses 10–15)

Good intentions resemble buds and blossoms: they are pleasant and give promise of fruit.

But if they produce no actual good deeds, their promise comes to nothing.

A good beginning is valuable, yet its benefit is lost without perseverance.

When people sincerely intend to do good and act according to the resources and abilities they possess, God does not reject them for what they cannot do.

But this does not excuse anyone who imagines that good intentions or merely claiming willingness is enough for salvation or for performing duty.

God's providence distributes earthly possessions unequally.

Some have much; others have little.

Those with abundance are therefore able to help people who lack necessities.

God intends that by supplying one another's needs, there should be a kind of equality.

Henry expressly rejects a forced leveling that would destroy private ownership; such a system, he argues, would remove the opportunity for voluntary generosity.

Everyone should feel responsible to help those in need.

Paul illustrates the point through the gathering and distribution of manna in the wilderness (Exodus 16:18).

In the end, even the wealthiest person needs only the ordinary necessities of life—food and clothing—while many who possess little still receive those necessities.

Paul recommended the brothers entrusted with receiving and carrying the gift so that the Corinthians would know whom they could trust.

Christians have a duty to act prudently and remove unnecessary grounds for suspicion.

It is essential to behave honestly before God.

But we should also take appropriate care to appear honest before other people, so that our integrity is visible and our usefulness is not hindered.

A clear public reputation and a pure conscience are both valuable for effective service.

The men commended by Paul glorified Christ through their work.

They were honored by him as faithful servants entrusted with his service.

When others place confidence in us, we should regard that confidence as a further reason to act well.

Seek God's approval, not self-congratulation (verses 12–18)

Comparing ourselves with people who surpass us can help keep us humble.

Paul adopted a better standard than the self-praise of his opponents.

He would speak only about the responsibility and field of service God had actually assigned him, not boast beyond his appointed measure.

Few things lead to so much error as judging people and opinions through our own prejudices.

How often people assess their religious character according to the expectations and values of the world around them!

But God's word provides a different standard.

Among all forms of flattery, self-flattery is the most dangerous.

Instead of praising ourselves, we should strive to be approved by God.

Our boasting belongs in the Lord who saves us.

We should value other things only as evidence of his love or as opportunities to advance his glory.

Rather than seeking the applause of people, let us desire the honor that comes from God alone.

Chapter 10
Chapter Outline
The apostle states his authority with meekness and humility. | (1-6) |
Reasons with the Corinthians. | (7-11) |
Seeks the glory of God, and to be approved of him. | (12-18) |
Verses 1-6
While others thought meanly, and spake scornfully of the apostle, he had low thoughts, and spake humbly of himself. We should be aware of our own infirmities, and think humbly of ourselves, even when men reproach us. The work of the ministry is a spiritual warfare with spiritual enemies, and for spiritual purposes. Outward force is not the method of the gospel, but strong persuasions, by the power of truth and the meekness of wisdom. Conscience is accountable to God only; and people must be persuaded to God and their duty, not driven by force. Thus the weapons of our warfare are very powerful; the evidence of truth is convincing. What opposition is made against the gospel, by the powers of sin and Satan in the hearts of men! But observe the conquest the word of God gains. The appointed means, however feeble they appear to some, will be mighty through God. And the preaching of the cross, by men of faith and prayer, has always been fatal to idolatry, impiety, and wickedness.
[2Cor.10.7-2Cor.10.11]
Verses 7-11
In outward appearance, Paul was mean and despised in the eyes of some, but this was a false rule to judge by. We must not think that none outward appearance, as if the want of such things proved a man not to be a real Christian, or an able, faithful minister of the lowly Saviour.
[2Cor.10.12-2Cor.10.18]
Verses 12-18
If we would compare ourselves with others who excel us, this would be a good method to keep us humble. The apostle fixes a good rule for his conduct; namely, not to boast of things without his measure, which was the measure God had distributed to him. There is not a more fruitful source of error, than to judge of persons and opinions by our own prejudices. How common is it for persons to judge of their own religious character, by the opinions and maxims of the world around them! But how different is the rule of God's word! And of all flattery, self-flattery is the worst. Therefore, instead of praising ourselves, we should strive to approve ourselves to God. In a word, let us glory in the Lord our salvation, and in all other things only as evidences of his love, or means of promoting his glory. Instead of praising ourselves, or seeking the praise of men, let us desire that honour which cometh from God only.
